stem: An online store uses Amazon DynamoDB for its orders table. The partition key of the table is CustomerId, and the sort key is OrderDate. A new screen in the application must list the orders of one customer sorted by OrderTotal. The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: currently holds two years of orders

options.text: Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: You can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to a table that holds data, and [the table continues to be available](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-add-to-existing-table) during the build.

options.text: Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: The table already holds orders, and you [cannot add a local secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to an existing table.

options.text: Scan the table with a filter expression on CustomerId for each request, and sort the returned orders by OrderTotal in the application.
options.why: It works, but a Scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without a filter, so each screen reads every order.

options.text: Copy each order into a second table keyed by CustomerId and OrderTotal through a Lambda function that reads the stream of the table.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and runs a function and a second table, while [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).
options.misconception: builds a copy table by hand where an index does the same job

explanation: The new query keeps CustomerId as the partition key but needs another sort key, and the table already holds data. You can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) at any time, and its [index key schema can be different](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-key-schema-can-differ) from the table. Queries on it [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi), which the screen accepts.
takeaway: For a new query on a table that already holds data, add a global secondary index.
twin: If the stem said "The table is being created now, and the new screen must use strongly consistent reads." instead: a local secondary index, because it is [created when the table is created](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-created-with-table).
say: The table already has data, so I'd add a GSI with CustomerId and OrderTotal; an LSI can't be added later.

stem: A company runs its order service in us-east-1 and stores the orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode in the same Region. The company is planning cross-Region disaster recovery for a failure of the whole Region. If us-east-1 fails, users must keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately, with no restore step. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add a replica table in us-west-2 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: [Any global table replica](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes) can [serve reads and writes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes), and a global table gives an [RTO of zero](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero), so us-west-2 takes the orders at once.

options.text: Use AWS Backup to back up the table every hour, and copy each backup to a backup vault in us-west-2 for restores.
options.why: A backup is restored into a new table before anyone can use it, and hourly copies give an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), not writes in us-west-2 at once.

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add replica tables in us-west-2 and in eu-west-1 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: It works, but the eu-west-1 replica table adds [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write, which no requirement needs.

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in us-west-2 that caches the items of the table and serves them to the application during an outage.
options.why: A DAX cluster can work only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so a cluster in us-west-2 cannot serve this table.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in another Region can stand in for the table

explanation: Users need to write in us-west-2 at once, with no restore step. A global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), so no database failover is needed, and replication gives an [RPO of a few seconds](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero). One replica table in us-west-2 meets the need at the lowest cost.
takeaway: Reads and writes in a second Region at once: a global table with one replica table there.
twin: If the stem said "If us-east-1 fails, a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable, and so is losing up to 1 hour of data." instead: AWS Backup with hourly copies, for an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour).

stem: A company runs a voting application that stores each vote as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. The partition key is the contest ID, and the application shows the running total of each contest. During a televised final, almost every vote is for one contest. Amazon CloudWatch shows that consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned write capacity of the table, but many writes are throttled. The company needs a scalable design. Which solution will BEST resolve the throttling?
keywords: almost every vote is for one contest
far below the provisioned write capacity

options.text: Raise the provisioned write capacity of the table to several times the current peak, and keep the contest ID as the partition key of every vote.
options.why: The table already has spare capacity; the limit is one partition, which delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) whatever the table total is.

options.text: Add a random number from a fixed range to the contest ID on each write, then query each suffix and sum the results to count the votes.
options.why: Random suffixes [randomize the writes across the larger space](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) of keys, and a total needs one query per suffix before you [merge the results](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-read-merge).

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that the table scales automatically with the burst of votes, and keep the contest ID as the partition key.
options.why: On-demand mode changes billing, not the partition ceiling of [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput), so the one hot contest is still throttled.

options.text: Make a unique vote ID the partition key of every item, and count the votes of a contest with a Scan that filters on the contest ID.
options.why: It ends the throttling, but in a Scan [DynamoDB reads every item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), so each running total reads the whole table.
options.misconception: fixes the writes with a design that makes every total a full table read

explanation: Consumed capacity is far below provisioned capacity, so the table is not short of capacity; one partition key is. A partition delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput), and [concentrated traffic that exceeds these limits](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-hot-partitions-throttle-while-others-underutilized) is throttled. Write sharding spreads one contest [across more distinct partition key values](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-few-partition-keys-spread-writes), so no single partition takes the whole burst.
takeaway: Throttling with spare table capacity means a hot partition key: spread it with a random suffix.
twin: If the stem said "consumed write capacity equals the provisioned write capacity, and the votes are spread across many contests" instead: raise the provisioned write capacity, because the table as a whole is short of capacity.
say: Spare capacity plus throttling means one hot key, so I'd shard the key with a random suffix.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that BEST resolves the throttling.

I mark the constraints: almost every vote is for one contest, the contest ID is the partition key, consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned capacity, and the application shows a running total per contest.
Before I look at the options, I predict a change of the partition key, because throttling with spare table capacity points to one hot key, and a random suffix spreads that key.

I remove the higher provisioned capacity, because the table already has spare capacity and each partition has its own ceiling. I remove on-demand mode, because it changes billing, not the ceiling of one partition.

Between the random suffix and the unique vote ID the difference is how the totals are read; the stem needs a running total per contest, so a Scan of the whole table for each total is the weaker design.
Check: the random suffix spreads the writes, a total needs one query per suffix, and every constraint is met. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A gaming company stores player profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The game reads the same small set of profile items thousands of times each second, and every read is eventually consistent. Reads take a few milliseconds today, and the company wants them to return in microseconds. The company wants to do this without changing the application's data access logic. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: same small set of profile items

options.text: Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and add code that reads each profile from the cache first and writes it to the cache after a miss.
options.why: It works, but the developers write cache-aside code, while DAX needs [only minimal functional changes](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes) for the same reads.
options.misconception: chooses a general cache that needs new caching code for DynamoDB reads

options.text: Raise the provisioned read capacity of the table to twice the current peak so that each profile read has more capacity to use.
options.why: Capacity sets how many reads the table accepts, not how fast each one returns, and DynamoDB alone gives [single-digit millisecond performance](../facts/dax.md#dax-modest-needs-use-dynamodb-alone).
options.misconception: believes that more read capacity makes each read faster

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for the table, and replace the DynamoDB client in the game with the DAX client.
options.why: DAX is [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes) and returns [eventually consistent data](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) [with microsecond latency](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency), so the game changes its client, not its calls.

options.text: Move the player profiles into an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and delete the DynamoDB table so that every read comes from memory.
options.why: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), so with the table deleted, the profiles lose their durable store.

explanation: The reads repeat, are eventually consistent and need microseconds, which is the DAX pattern. DAX fits applications that [read a small number of items more frequently](../facts/dax.md#dax-ideal-fastest-reads-hot-keys) than others. It is [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes), so the game keeps its data access calls and swaps the client.
takeaway: Repeated eventually consistent DynamoDB reads that need microseconds: add DAX and swap the client.
twin: If the stem said "every profile read must be strongly consistent" instead: DAX does not help, because [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions).

stem: A company stores product items in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. Every item is 6 KB in size. The application needs to make 100 strongly consistent reads per second and 50 writes per second on these items. None of the writes are part of a transaction. A solutions architect needs to set the provisioned capacity of the table to match this load. How many read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) does the table need?

options.text: 100 RCUs and 300 WCUs
options.why: This prices each read like an eventually consistent read, but a unit gives [one strongly consistent read operation per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-rcu-definition) per block, so these reads need twice as many units.
options.misconception: prices each strongly consistent read like an eventually consistent read

options.text: 200 RCUs and 50 WCUs
options.why: This counts one unit per write, but a unit covers [one write per second for an item up to 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wcu-definition), so a larger item takes more units.

options.text: 150 RCUs and 300 WCUs
options.why: This divides the item size by the read block without rounding up, but sizes round up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb) before the division.
options.misconception: divides the item size by the read block without rounding up

options.text: 200 RCUs and 300 WCUs
options.why: A read rounds up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb), so each strongly consistent read takes two units; each write takes six units, because you [divide the item size of the operation by 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-capacity-formula).

explanation: For reads, you [divide the item size of the operation by 4 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-formula) and round up, so each strongly consistent read takes two units. For writes, you [divide the item size of the operation by 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-capacity-formula), so each write takes six units. Multiply each by the request rates in the stem.
takeaway: Reads round up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb) and writes to the [next 1 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-rounding-1kb); then multiply by the rate.
twin: If the stem said "100 eventually consistent reads per second" instead: half the read units, because one RCU gives [two eventually consistent read operations per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-rcu-definition).

stem: An online store uses Amazon DynamoDB for its orders table. The partition key of the table is CustomerId, and the sort key is OrderDate. A new screen in the application must list the orders of one customer sorted by OrderTotal. The table is being created now, and the new screen must use strongly consistent reads. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: The screen needs strongly consistent reads, but queries on a global secondary index [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi).

options.text: Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: The table is new, so the index is [created when the table is created](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-created-with-table), and a query can use [either eventually consistent or strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-strongly-consistent-allowed).

options.text: Scan the table with a filter expression on CustomerId for each request, and sort the returned orders by OrderTotal in the application.
options.why: It works, but a Scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without a filter, so each screen reads every order.

options.text: Copy each order into a second table keyed by CustomerId and OrderTotal through a Lambda function that reads the stream of the table.
options.why: The copy is written from the stream after each change, and [reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-and-streams-reads-eventual), so the copy can miss the latest write.
options.misconception: treats a copy that is written after each change as current

explanation: The screen needs strong reads on another sort key of the same customer. A local secondary index has the [same partition key as the base table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-same-partition-key) and its own sort key. Strongly consistent reads are [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi), and the table is new, so the index can be defined now.
takeaway: Strong reads on another sort key of a new table: define a local secondary index at creation.
twin: If the stem said "The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable." instead: a global secondary index, because you can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) later.

stem: A company stores support tickets as items in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Agents update each ticket many times during its life. When the status of a ticket changes to CLOSED, the company must send a satisfaction survey email to the customer in near real-time. The solution must not send a second email when an agent edits a ticket that is already closed. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: status of a ticket changes to CLOSED

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and have an AWS Lambda function read the stream records once a week and email every ticket that was closed that week.
options.why: Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), so a weekly job misses most changes, and the emails are days late.

options.text: Run an AWS Lambda function every minute on an Amazon EventBridge schedule that scans the table for closed tickets and emails the ones not yet emailed.
options.why: It works, but each run reads the whole table, because in a Scan [DynamoDB reads every item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), and the code tracks the emails it sent.
options.misconception: polls the whole table instead of reacting to each item change

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams with new and old item images, and add an AWS Lambda trigger that emails when the status changes to CLOSED.
options.why: A trigger can [automatically respond to events in DynamoDB Streams](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-lambda-triggers), and the record holds [both the new and the old images](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-view-new-and-old-images), so the function sees the change to CLOSED.

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and run an application on Amazon EC2 instances that polls the stream of the table and sends the survey emails.
options.why: It can work, but the team runs, patches and scales instances, while a Lambda trigger needs no servers to manage.
options.misconception: runs its own stream reader on instances where a managed trigger exists

explanation: The email follows one item change. DynamoDB Streams records a [time-ordered sequence of every item-level change](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-time-ordered-changes) in [near-real time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-time-ordered-changes), and a stream has a [native integration with AWS Lambda](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-streams-lambda-triggers). The old image shows whether the ticket was already closed, so an edit of a closed ticket sends no second email.
takeaway: Run code on each item change with a stream and a Lambda trigger; keep old images to compare.
twin: If the stem said "an audit job must replay every status change of the last 7 days" instead: Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, because it keeps records [up to 1 year](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-retention).

stem: An online store keeps its product catalog in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Product pages read the same popular items thousands of times each second. For the product pages, data that is a few seconds old is acceptable, and reads must return in microseconds. At checkout, the application must read the current price of each item with a strongly consistent read. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
keywords: a few seconds old is acceptable

options.text: Copy the popular items into the memory of each web server, refresh the copies every few seconds, and read checkout prices from the table.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds and refreshes a cache on every web server, while DAX is managed and [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes).
options.misconception: builds a cache by hand on each server where a managed cache exists

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster, send all reads through the DAX client, and make every read strongly consistent so that checkout uses the cache too.
options.why: DAX passes a strongly consistent read on, and [it does not cache the results](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions), so the product pages lose their microsecond reads.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for the product pages, and read checkout prices from a global secondary index with strongly consistent reads.
options.why: Strongly consistent reads are [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi), so a global secondary index cannot return the current price.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster, send all reads through the DAX client, and use eventually consistent reads for pages and strongly consistent reads at checkout.
options.why: DAX serves [eventually consistent data](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) [with microsecond latency](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) to the pages, and [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions) for checkout.

explanation: The deciding phrases are microsecond page reads and strong reads at checkout. The DAX client [directs all of your application's DynamoDB API requests](../facts/dax.md#dax-client-routes-requests-to-cluster) to the cluster. Eventually consistent page reads come from the cache, and [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions), so checkout reads the current price from the table.
takeaway: DAX caches eventually consistent reads and passes strongly consistent reads to the table.
twin: If the stem said "every read, on the pages and at checkout, must be strongly consistent" instead: DAX adds nothing, because for those reads [it does not cache the results](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions).

stem: A company runs its order service in us-east-1 and stores the orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode in the same Region. The company is planning cross-Region disaster recovery for a failure of the whole Region. If us-east-1 fails, a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable, and so is losing up to 1 hour of data. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable
losing up to 1 hour of data

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add a replica table in us-west-2 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: It works, but the replica table bills [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write all day, for a recovery speed that the stem does not ask for.

options.text: Use AWS Backup to back up the table every hour, and copy each backup to a backup vault in us-west-2 for restores.
options.why: AWS Backup plans can copy backups across Regions [every hour, every 12 hours, daily, weekly, or monthly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), and the hourly copy gives an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour).

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add replica tables in us-west-2 and in eu-west-1 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: It works, but two replica tables each bill [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write, far more than hourly backups cost.

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in us-west-2 that caches the items of the table and serves them to the application during an outage.
options.why: A DAX cluster can work only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so a cluster in us-west-2 cannot serve this table.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in another Region can stand in for the table

explanation: The stem accepts an hour of data loss and a restore that takes hours, so continuous replication is not needed. Hourly AWS Backup copies to us-west-2 give an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour). After an outage, you restore the [entire table data to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-backup-restore-only-to-new-table) in us-west-2.
takeaway: When hours of recovery and an hour of data loss are acceptable, cross-Region backups cost less than a global table.
twin: If the stem said "If us-east-1 fails, users must keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately, with no restore step." instead: a global table, because it gives an [RTO of zero](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero).

stem: A company will open ticket sales for a large concert at a fixed time next week. The tickets are stored in a new Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode, and the table has served only light test traffic so far. At the opening minute, the company expects a peak of many times more requests than the table has ever served. The company has stringent requirements: no request can be throttled. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: has served only light test traffic

options.text: Before the sale, raise the warm throughput of the table to the expected peak so that the table can serve that rate at once.
options.why: [Pre-warming](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events) raises warm throughput ahead of time and sets a [baseline that your tables can instantly support](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events), so the opening peak is served.

options.text: Keep the table in on-demand capacity mode without other changes, because on-demand capacity mode serves any number of requests the moment they arrive.
options.why: On-demand mode [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double); above that, [throttling can occur](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-throttle-if-double-within-30-min), and this jump is far larger.

options.text: Switch the table to provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling at a 70% target utilization, and let auto scaling add capacity during the sale.
options.why: Auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible), so requests in the opening minute are throttled before the new capacity arrives.

options.text: Run a load script in the days before the sale that sends test traffic which keeps doubling until the table has served the expected peak.
options.why: It can work, because the table then has a higher previous peak, but the team runs load tests for days instead of changing one table setting.
options.misconception: raises the previous peak by hand with synthetic traffic

explanation: The table has served only light traffic, and on-demand mode [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double). Warm throughput is what a table [can instantaneously support](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition). Raising it before the sale, called [pre-warming](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events), prepares the table for the known peak with one change.
takeaway: A known launch far above any earlier peak: pre-warm the table by raising its warm throughput.
twin: If the stem said "a peak about the same as the busiest day the table has already served" instead: keep on-demand mode, because it [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double).

stem: A company runs a profile service for users around the world. The service stores user profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table in us-east-1. Users in Europe and Asia report slow saves, because every write travels to us-east-1. Each write must be served in the user's own Region, and the service must stay highly available if one Region fails. Which solution provides the LOWEST latency for writes from every user?
keywords: served in the user's own Region

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, send every write to the replica table in us-east-1, and fail writes over to another Region in an outage.
options.why: It works, but a global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), so sending every write to us-east-1 keeps the slow writes for Europe and Asia.

options.text: Migrate the profiles to an Amazon Aurora global database with a cluster in each user Region, and send each write to the cluster in that Region.
options.why: In an Aurora global database, [only the primary cluster performs write operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer), so the clusters in Europe and Asia cannot accept local writes.

options.text: Convert the table into a global table with replica tables in the Regions of the users, and have each Region write to its local replica table.
options.why: [Any global table replica](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes) can [serve reads and writes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes), so each user writes to a nearby replica table with [fast local read and write performance](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-tables-definition).

options.text: Create DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in Europe and in Asia that cache the table and accept the profile writes of local users.
options.why: A DAX cluster works only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so clusters in Europe and Asia cannot serve a table in us-east-1.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in another Region can take writes for the table

explanation: The deciding phrase is local writes in every Region. Global tables are a [multi-Region, and multi-active database](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-multi-active), so every replica table accepts writes near its users. If one Region fails, the others keep serving reads and writes, because a global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed).
takeaway: Local writes in many Regions: a DynamoDB global table, where every replica table accepts writes.
twin: If the stem said "users in Europe and Asia only read profiles, and the data is relational" instead: an Aurora global database, with [up to 10 read-only secondary AWS Regions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer) for local reads.
